sections.section_title: Restoring the Fallen and Testing One's Own Work
sections.summary: The neutral reading finds that Paul instructs the Spirit-led community on how to restore a member who has been caught in transgression, warns the restorer of equal vulnerability, commands mutual burden-bearing as fulfillment of the law of Christ, and establishes individual eschatological accountability before God.
sections.relevance: The passage assumes that believers can genuinely fall into transgression and require communal restoration, while the warning 'lest you too be tempted' dissolves any presumption of invulnerability among the 'spiritual.' The eschatological dimension of verse 5 — 'each will have to bear his own load' — establishes individual accountability before God for one's own conduct, implying that the outcome of that accountability is not predetermined regardless of behavior. Though the passage addresses community ethics rather than standing before God directly, the framework of real vulnerability, real falling, and real eschatological reckoning bears on the conditionality question.
key_phrases: if anyone is caught in any transgression
restore him in a spirit of gentleness
each will have to bear his own load

sections.summary: The neutral reading finds that Paul instructs those receiving oral teaching to share material goods with their teachers, establishing a reciprocal relationship of spiritual instruction and material support.

sections.section_title: The Sowing-Reaping Principle — Flesh and Spirit in Eschatological Terms
sections.summary: The neutral reading finds that Paul restates the flesh-Spirit contrast in agricultural and eschatological terms: sowing to the flesh reaps corruption, sowing to the Spirit reaps eternal life, and the harvest is conditioned on perseverance — 'if we do not give up.'
sections.relevance: The neutral reading explicitly identifies this passage as continuing the warning trajectory of 5:4 (severed from Christ) and 5:21 (will not inherit the kingdom): 'All three warnings are addressed to believers. All three describe real possibilities. The inheritance — the kingdom of God, eternal life — is genuine, but it is not automatically guaranteed regardless of subsequent choices.' The sowing-reaping principle makes the Galatians' present decisions the determinative factor in their eschatological outcome — eternal life or corruption. The conditional clause 'if we do not give up' (me eklyomenoi) directly conditions the promised harvest on perseverance, and the neutral reading states: 'the harvest is certain for those who persist, but those who give up will not receive it.' This is Paul's own argument, not an illustration or aside, and it directly addresses the believer's ultimate standing by tying it to ongoing conduct and perseverance.
key_phrases: whatever one sows, that will he also reap
the one who sows to his own flesh will from the flesh reap corruption
the one who sows to the Spirit will from the Spirit reap eternal life
if we do not give up
let us not grow weary of doing good

sections.section_title: Paul's Handwritten Summary — The Cross Against Circumcision
sections.summary: The neutral reading finds that Paul's handwritten summary exposes the agitators' motives as vanity and cowardice, contrasts their flesh-boasting with his cross-boasting, declares that neither circumcision nor uncircumcision counts for anything but only new creation, and presents his own scars as authenticating marks of belonging to Jesus.
sections.relevance: The passage bears on the question indirectly but significantly. The agitators are actively compelling believers to accept circumcision (6:12), which per the letter's established argument (5:4) results in severance from Christ and falling from grace. The text assumes that believers can be pressured into choosing the flesh-system over the cross, and that this choice has consequences for their standing. The declaration that what matters is 'new creation' (6:15) — not circumcision status — establishes the operative category of standing before God, and the implied corollary is that abandoning the new-creation reality for the flesh-system means forfeiting that standing. Paul's 'the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world' (6:14) models the decisive break with the old system, but the letter's entire occasion is that the Galatians are being tempted to reverse that break.
key_phrases: those who want to make a good showing in the flesh
they may not be persecuted for the cross of Christ
they desire to have you circumcised that they may boast in your flesh
far be it from me to boast except in the cross
the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world
neither circumcision counts for anything, nor uncircumcision, but a new creation

sections.summary: The neutral reading finds that Paul closes the letter with a grace-benediction that invokes the word charis — the sphere from which the Galatians were called, into which they were summoned, and from which they risk falling — and addresses the Galatians as 'brothers' despite the letter's severity.
